text: The Jensen Interceptor was introduced in 1950 as the second car produced by Jensen Motors after World War II, based on Austin components with a body crafted by Jensen and styled by Eric Neale. It featured a 3,993 cc (4.0 L; 243.7 cu in) straight-six engine and transmission from the Austin Sheerline, along with a chassis derived from the Austin A70 and modified independent coil sprung suspension. Production ran through 1957, and the name was later reused for a second-generation Jensen Interceptor launched in 1966, with subsequent revivals. The car initially debuted as a convertible with a mix of aluminium and steel on a wood frame, featuring a hinged front section for engine access and a rigid plastic (Perspex) wrap-around rear window that dropped into a well when the top was lowered. In 1952, a hardtop with a fabric-covered roof and a few sedan versions were introduced. Total production included 32 convertibles, 52 saloons, and 4 sedancas. The braking system initially used a mixed Girling hydraulic/mechanical setup, later upgraded to a full hydraulic system, while the four-speed manual transmission gained an optional overdrive in 1952, which required a 3.77:1 rear axle ratio. A 1952 convertible tested by The Motor achieved a top speed of 95 mph (153 km/h), accelerating from 0-60 mph (97 km/h) in 17.8 seconds with a fuel consumption of 20.3 miles per gallon (imperial). In 1952, the car was priced at £2645 (including tax) on the home market, with the overdrive adding an extra £116. In 1953, American race car legend Briggs Cunningham owned a left-hand drive Interceptor fitted with a 331 cu in (5.4 L), 180 bhp (134.2 kW) Chrysler "Firepower" hemi engine, achieving a top speed approaching 145 mph and ranking as the second fastest production car of 1955, behind the Mercedes-Benz 300SL. Jensen also produced the Austin A40 Sports, a smaller vehicle that resembled a scaled-down version of the Interceptor.
